abstract: Known for their rapid water surface locomotion, whirligig beetles (Gyrinidae) are also fast divers. They can transition from the surface to underwater swimming in under 100 ms. Diving requires them to generate sufficient hydrodynamic torque to break the water surface and reorient the body. However, the mechanism by which whirligigs create the necessary pitch-down torque is unknown. Here, we show that their diving is achieved by bending the abdomen. The inertial hydrodynamic pressure on the flexed abdomen generates the torque necessary for surface breaking and body rotation. The torque is maximized at an abdominal angle of 45{degrees}, whereas for effective diving, whirligigs display a preferential abdominal angle of around 28{degrees}, closely aligning with the angle that maximizes the torque-to-drag ratio. This abdominal angle is optimized by balancing torque generation with the drag penalty. Our findings inspire a mechanism for surface-to-underwater transition, offering design principles for multimodal robots capable of locomotion across the air-water interface.
